subject: Medicine
topic: Adult Pneumococcal Immunization Recommendations
stem:
A 66-year-old woman presents to the ambulatory internal medicine clinic for a routine annual preventive health examination. She has a history of mild osteoarthritis of the hands but has no chronic heart, lung, liver, or renal disease, and does not have diabetes mellitus. She does not use immunosuppressive medications and has never undergone splenectomy. She has never received any pneumococcal vaccine. Vital signs and physical examination are completely normal.

According to current Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) guidelines, which of the following represents the recommended pneumococcal vaccination strategy for this patient?

options.text: Administer a single dose of 20-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV20) alone, OR administer a single dose of 15-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV15) followed at least 1 year later by a dose of 23-valent pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23)
options.explanation: The Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) updated adult pneumococcal immunization guidelines following the licensure of higher-valency pneumococcal conjugate vaccines: (1) TARGET POPULATION: All immunocompetent adults >= 65 years of age who have not previously received a pneumococcal conjugate vaccine or whose vaccination history is unknown. (2) SIMPLIFIED TWO-OPTION REGIMEN: (a) OPTION 1 (PREFERRED FOR SIMPLICITY): Administer a SINGLE DOSE of 20-valent Pneumococcal Conjugate Vaccine (PCV20) alone. No subsequent pneumococcal vaccines (such as PPSV23) are required following PCV20 because PCV20 provides broader conjugate coverage and induces robust T-cell-dependent immunological memory. (b) OPTION 2: Administer a single dose of 15-valent Pneumococcal Conjugate Vaccine (PCV15) FOLLOWED by a dose of 23-valent Pneumococcal Polysaccharide Vaccine (PPSV23) administered AT LEAST 1 YEAR LATER (an interval of >= 8 weeks can be used for immunocompromised patients, but >= 1 year is standard for immunocompetent adults >= 65). (3) OBSOLESCENCE OF HISTORICAL REGIMENS: Historical regimens utilizing PCV13 followed by PPSV23 in series are no longer recommended for vaccine-naive adults because PCV15 and PCV20 contain serotypes with higher contemporary disease burden. PPSV23 should NEVER be given alone as initial monotherapy in conjugate-naive adults.

options.text: Administer a single dose of 23-valent pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23) alone, with no conjugate vaccine needed
options.explanation: PPSV23 alone induces T-cell-independent B-cell responses without immunological memory; ACIP guidelines mandate a conjugate vaccine (PCV20 or PCV15) as the foundation of adult vaccination.

options.text: Administer 13-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV13) followed 8 weeks later by PCV20
options.explanation: PCV13 has been replaced by PCV15 and PCV20; furthermore, giving two conjugate vaccines in series is redundant and contrary to ACIP recommendations.

options.text: Withhold pneumococcal vaccination until age 75 unless high-risk immunocompromising conditions develop
options.explanation: Pneumococcal immunization is universally recommended for all adults beginning at age 65 regardless of medical conditions, due to age-related immunosenescence and high invasive pneumococcal disease risk.

options.text: Administer PCV20 followed 8 weeks later by a mandatory booster dose of PPSV23
options.explanation: When PCV20 is administered, no subsequent dose of PPSV23 is indicated; PCV20 is complete as a standalone single-dose vaccination.

topic: Colorectal Cancer Screening Modalities and Age Thresholds
stem:
A 46-year-old man presents to the primary care clinic for an annual preventive checkup. He has no chronic medical conditions, takes no medications, and feels completely well. He has no gastrointestinal symptoms, changes in bowel habits, rectal bleeding, unexplained weight loss, or abdominal pain. Review of family history reveals that his parents and two siblings are healthy, with no family history of colorectal cancer, advanced adenomas, inflammatory bowel disease, or hereditary cancer syndromes (Lynch syndrome or familial adenomatous polyposis). Physical examination is normal. The patient asks whether he needs screening for colorectal cancer.

According to current US Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) guidelines, which of the following represents the most appropriate colorectal cancer screening recommendation for this average-risk patient?

options.text: Defer all colorectal cancer screening until age 50, as routine screening prior to age 50 is not cost-effective or recommended for average-risk individuals
options.explanation: The USPSTF officially lowered the screening initiation age to 45 years in 2021; deferring screening until age 50 misses early resectable neoplasia in young adults.

options.text: Initiate routine colorectal cancer screening now (at age 45) using any of the guideline-approved screening strategies (e.g., optical colonoscopy every 10 years, annual fecal immunochemical test [FIT], or stool FIT-DNA every 3 years), with the understanding that any positive non-colonoscopic screening test mandates a timely diagnostic colonoscopy
options.explanation: Colorectal Cancer (CRC) is the third leading cause of cancer-related mortality in the United States. (1) USPSTF 2021 UPDATED SCREENING RECOMMENDATION: The USPSTF lowered the recommended age to INITIATE ROUTINE SCREENING FROM AGE 50 TO AGE 45 for all average-risk adults (Grade B recommendation for ages 45-49, Grade A for ages 50-75). This shift was driven by robust epidemiological modeling demonstrating a dramatic, progressive rise in young-onset colorectal cancer incidence over the past two decades. (2) APPROVED SCREENING STRATEGIES AND INTERVALS: Several screening modalities have demonstrated clinical efficacy: (a) DIRECT VISUALIZATION TESTS: Optical colonoscopy every 10 years (the gold standard; allows simultaneous visualization and polypectomy of precancerous adenomas), or Flexible sigmoidoscopy every 5 years (or every 10 years plus annual FIT), or CT colonography every 5 years. (b) STOOL-BASED TESTS: Annual Fecal Immunochemical Test (FIT, high sensitivity for human globin), or Stool FIT-DNA (Cologuard, multi-target sDNA plus FIT) every 3 years, or annual high-sensitivity guaiac-based fecal occult blood test (gFOBT). (3) MANDATORY CLINICAL RULE FOR POSITIVE STOOL TESTS: If any non-invasive stool test (FIT, FIT-DNA) or CT colonography yields a positive result, A TIMELY DIAGNOSTIC COLONOSCOPY IS MANDATORY. Non-invasive tests are screening tools, not definitive diagnoses; failing to follow up a positive stool test with colonoscopy leads to delayed detection of advanced colorectal neoplasia.

options.text: If an annual fecal immunochemical test (FIT) is positive, repeat the FIT in 1 month and perform colonoscopy only if the second test is positive
options.explanation: Repeating a stool test after a positive result is a dangerous clinical error; any single positive FIT mandates immediate diagnostic colonoscopy to evaluate for colorectal cancer or large adenomas.

options.text: Perform optical colonoscopy every 5 years for average-risk individuals
options.explanation: For average-risk individuals with a completely normal screening colonoscopy, the recommended screening interval is 10 years, not 5 years; performing colonoscopy every 5 years represents overutilization.

options.text: Order serum carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) annually as a non-invasive screening modality
options.explanation: Serum CEA has poor sensitivity and specificity for early colorectal neoplasia and is strictly contraindicated as a screening test; CEA is used exclusively for monitoring recurrence in established disease.

stem:
A 56-year-old man presents to the clinic for a routine wellness visit. He has a 24 pack-year smoking history (smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for 24 years) but successfully quit smoking 8 years ago. He is completely asymptomatic and denies chronic cough, hemoptysis, shortness of breath, chest pain, or unintentional weight loss. His past medical history includes mild hypertension well controlled with hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily. Vital signs demonstrate blood pressure of 124/76 mm Hg, heart rate of 70/min, and oxygen saturation of 98% on room air. Physical examination reveals clear lungs to auscultation bilaterally. He has no other chronic medical conditions and has an active, excellent functional performance status.

According to current US Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) guidelines, which of the following represents the most appropriate lung cancer screening recommendation for this patient?

options.text: Perform annual screening with a standard two-view posterior-anterior and lateral chest radiograph
options.explanation: Standard chest radiography (with or without sputum cytology) has no demonstrated efficacy in reducing lung cancer mortality in randomized trials and is explicitly recommended against by the USPSTF.

options.text: Withhold lung cancer screening because the patient has not smoked for > 5 years and has accumulated < 30 pack-years
options.explanation: Under the updated 2021 USPSTF criteria, the pack-year threshold was lowered to >= 20 pack-years and screening continues until 15 years post-quitting; this patient qualifies with 24 pack-years and 8 years since quitting.

options.text: Perform annual screening for lung cancer with low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) of the chest
options.explanation: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer mortality in both men and women in the United States. (1) USPSTF 2021 UPDATED SCREENING RECOMMENDATIONS: In 2021, the USPSTF expanded lung cancer screening eligibility based on the National Lung Screening Trial (NLST) and the NELSON trial: (a) AGE RANGE: Adults aged 50 to 80 years (expanded from prior 55-80); (b) SMOKING HISTORY THRESHOLD: A cumulative tobacco smoking history of >= 20 PACK-YEARS (lowered from prior 30 pack-years); AND (c) CURRENT SMOKER OR QUIT WITHIN THE PAST 15 YEARS. (2) PATIENT APPLICATION: This patient is 56 years of age (within 50-80), has a 24 pack-year smoking history (exceeds >= 20 pack-years), and quit 8 years ago (within the 15-year quit window). stem:
A 38-year-old woman presents to the ambulatory women's health clinic for a routine gynecological examination. She is asymptomatic, has no abnormal vaginal bleeding or discharge, and has had no postcoital spotting. She has a history of two uncomplicated term vaginal deliveries. She has no personal history of high-grade cervical dysplasia (cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or 3 [CIN 2/3]) or cervical cancer, is not immunocompromised, and has never had HIV infection. Review of her medical record reveals that her last cervical cancer screening was performed 5 years ago (at age 33), at which time she underwent cervical cytology (Papanicolaou smear) co-tested with high-risk human papillomavirus (hrHPV) testing; both tests were completely negative. Physical and speculum examinations reveal a normal, smooth cervix without lesions or contact bleeding.

According to current US Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) and American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) guidelines, which of the following represents an acceptable screening strategy for this patient today?

options.text: Annual cervical cytology (Pap smear) combined with high-risk HPV testing performed every year
options.explanation: Annual cervical cancer screening in an average-risk woman with prior negative tests represents overtreatment, leading to high false-positive rates, unnecessary colposcopies, and cervical procedural harms.

options.text: Perform an immediate diagnostic colposcopy with directed cervical biopsies rather than non-invasive screening
options.explanation: Colposcopy is a diagnostic procedure indicated only after an abnormal screening test (e.g., persistent HPV 16/18 or ASC-H/HSIL); it is never used as routine primary screening.

options.text: Discontinue all cervical cancer screening, as having two prior normal screenings provides lifelong immunity against cervical dysplasia

topic: Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA) Screening and Surgical Repair Indications
stem:
A 67-year-old man presents to the clinic for a routine checkup. He feels completely healthy, is asymptomatic, and has no abdominal or back pain. His medical history includes essential hypertension treated with amlodipine 5 mg daily. He has a 35 pack-year smoking history (smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily from age 20 to 55) but successfully quit 12 years ago. Physical examination demonstrates blood pressure of 128/78 mm Hg and heart rate of 72/min. Abdominal examination reveals a soft, non-tender abdomen with a wide, prominent, pulsatile midline mass palpated in the epigastric region measuring approximately 4.5 cm in width. Peripheral pulses are normal.

According to current US Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) and Society for Vascular Surgery (SVS) guidelines, which of the following represents the most appropriate screening and management strategy for abdominal aortic aneurysm in this patient?

options.text: Perform an emergent open surgical laparotomy today for immediate aortic graft placement based on physical examination alone
options.explanation: Physical examination has poor diagnostic accuracy and overestimates aortic diameter; non-invasive ultrasound imaging is required first, and elective repair is indicated only for diameter >= 5.5 cm or symptoms.

options.text: Perform non-contrast abdominal computed tomography (CT) annually for all patients with a history of hypertension regardless of smoking history
options.explanation: Annual CT scans expose patients to unnecessary cumulative ionizing radiation, and screening is not recommended based on hypertension alone without a smoking history.

options.text: Withhold all vascular imaging because the patient successfully quit smoking 12 years ago
options.explanation: USPSTF guidelines define 'ever-smoker' as >= 100 lifetime cigarettes regardless of when smoking ceased; quitting 12 years ago does not remove the mandate for one-time ultrasound screening.

options.text: Order a one-time screening abdominal ultrasound and recommend immediate elective surgical repair if the aortic diameter reaches 3.5 cm
options.explanation: At 3.5 cm, the annual risk of rupture is virtually 0%, whereas surgical repair carries a 1-5% perioperative mortality; surgical repair at 3.5 cm represents dangerous overtreatment (threshold is >= 5.5 cm).

options.text: Perform a one-time screening abdominal duplex ultrasound to evaluate for abdominal aortic aneurysm, and schedule elective surgical or endovascular repair if the maximal infrarenal aortic diameter is >= 5.5 cm or expands > 0.5 cm in 6 months
options.explanation: Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA) is defined as a focal permanent dilation of the abdominal aorta >= 3.0 cm in maximal transverse diameter (or > 50% dilation compared to normal adjacent aorta), typically occurring in the infrarenal segment. (1) USPSTF SCREENING CRITERIA: A ONE-TIME SCREENING ABDOMINAL DUPLEX ULTRASOUND is recommended for MEN AGED 65 TO 75 YEARS WHO HAVE EVER SMOKED (defined as having smoked >= 100 lifetime cigarettes; Grade B recommendation). Ultrasound is the screening modality of choice with > 98% sensitivity and specificity, zero radiation exposure, and non-invasiveness. (2) SVS SURVEILLANCE INTERVALS: (a) Aorta 3.0 to 3.9 cm: Surveillance ultrasound every 3 years; (b) Aorta 4.0 to 4.9 cm: Surveillance ultrasound every 12 months; (c) Aorta 5.0 to 5.4 cm: Surveillance ultrasound or CT angiography every 6 months. (3) DEFINITIVE SURGICAL REPAIR INDICATIONS: Elective repair (Endovascular Aneurysm Repair [EVAR] or open surgical repair) is indicated when the rupture risk exceeds the procedural mortality risk: (a) MAXIMAL DIAMETER >= 5.5 CM IN MEN (or >= 5.0 cm in women); (b) RAPID EXPANSION: Defined as aortic diameter growth > 0.5 cm in 6 months or > 1.0 cm in 1 year; OR (c) ANY SYMPTOMATIC ANEURYSM (abdominal, flank, or back pain, or tender pulsatile mass), which represents impending rupture and mandates emergent repair regardless of diameter.
